speaker: Guillermo Rauch
title: A conversation with Vercel's Guillermo Rauch
question: In developer tools, how does treating AI coding agents as primary users change what makes a good developer experience?
guest: We think of the agent and how the agent is going to reason through this. A little example from literally last night: one of our framework builders who works on what we call agentic developer experience said, "What happens when agents use Next.js is that they will boot up lots of dev servers and kill them, and boot up lots of dev servers and kill them." This is not a behavior that a human does. A human boots up one, they go to work through their text editor, and that is it. Agents try lots of things really quickly, and if you give them rope, they will do a lot of stuff in parallel. So what we realized is that in one error message in Next.js, we had to include the process ID to give the agent context of what process to kill to recover the port that the previous process was using. This tiny amount of information—a hashtag and then the identifier of the process—makes a marginal difference for people, because an engineer would just run ps and grep by Next, but it makes a gigantic difference for agents. As developer tools advance, they will continue to cater to the LLM that calls tools and commands.

points.core: Coding agents rapidly cycle through parallel local processes unlike single-session human developers.
points.note: Accept: agents booting many dev servers, running parallel experiments, or rapidly restarting local processes rather than working in one persistent session. Do not credit: generic claims that AI codes faster than humans.

points.core: Error messages should surface explicit machine-actionable identifiers so agents can self-recover.
points.note: Accept: including process IDs, port owners, or structured diagnostic context in CLI errors so an agent can automatically fix conflicts without extra shell lookups. Do not credit: vague advice to write clearer error messages.

points.core: Tiny structured context additions improve agent reliability far more than human ergonomics.
points.note: Accept: small metadata tweaks making a marginal difference to humans (who can run ps/grep) but a massive reliability jump for tool-calling LLMs. Do not credit: generic statements about prompt engineering or good documentation.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Treating agents as primary users shifts good developer experience from visual polish and human intuition toward machine legibility, determinism, and fast feedback loops.

Agents don't browse dashboards or absorb tribal knowledge; they read text, call commands, and act on whatever comes back. So the things that matter most become: complete, accurate, plain-text documentation (and context files such as AGENTS.md or llms.txt); CLIs and APIs with structured, parseable output rather than GUI-only workflows; non-interactive modes with no prompts or hidden state; and error messages that state exactly what went wrong and how to fix it, since an agent will act on the error literally.

Verification also becomes central. Agents iterate by running things, so fast, reliable tests, type checkers, and linters effectively serve as the interface. Consistency and predictability beat cleverness, because surprising conventions that a human learns once will trip an agent every session. Safety features matter more too: scoped permissions, dry-run modes, sandboxes, and easy reversibility.

Most of this is also what humans always wanted; agents simply tolerate ambiguity and undocumented behaviour far less, and the human's role shifts toward reviewing and steering.

The response recommends parseable output and explicit fix instructions but does not connect identifiers or structured error details to autonomous recovery.
The response says agents tolerate less ambiguity but does not explain how a small metadata addition can greatly improve agent reliability while offering humans little benefit.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Treating AI coding agents as primary users shifts developer experience from visual ergonomics and human intuition toward machine legibility, tight verification loops, and safe autonomy. Whereas human developers benefit from interactive dashboards, setup wizards, and implicit conventions, agents thrive on deterministic, non-interactive CLIs, structured outputs like JSON, idempotent APIs, and explicit tool protocols that eliminate stateful prompts.

Documentation and context change accordingly: scattered web portals and narrative tutorials matter less than concise, versioned plain text, strict schemas, and strong type systems optimized for local discovery and token efficiency. Feedback speed and signal density also become paramount. Compilers, linters, and test suites must return sub-second, localized diagnostics with actionable remediation hints rather than noisy logs that flood context windows, turning every tool into an oracle for autonomous self-correction. Finally, agent-first tooling prioritizes cheap, ephemeral sandboxes, instant environment branching, dry-run modes, and granular permissions, letting agents experiment, verify behavior end-to-end, and recover from mistakes safely before human review.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Once AI agents are the main users of a tool, a good developer experience stops depending on visual polish and discoverability. What matters is whether a machine can read the tool, predict what it will do, and recover when something goes wrong.

Agents work from text and context windows, not dashboards. So the best tools offer structured, parseable output such as JSON modes and stable schemas. They also give actionable error messages that say what failed and how to fix it, and they keep documentation in plain text or Markdown (llms.txt files, for example) instead of behind JavaScript-heavy sites. Commands should be deterministic and idempotent, should run without interactive prompts, and should use consistent naming so an agent can generalize from one command to the next. Fast feedback loops become essential because agents improve through repeated attempts, which makes quick tests, type checks, linters and sandboxes central. Exposing capabilities through standard interfaces like CLIs, APIs or MCP servers matters more than a GUI. Safety becomes part of the design too, through scoped permissions, dry-run modes, reversible operations and audit logs. Humans still benefit from all of this, but the bar moves from "pleasant to use" to "unambiguous to automate."

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Treating AI coding agents as primary users shifts developer experience from human ergonomics toward machine legibility, determinism, and fast self-correction. Traditional tools prioritize visual polish, interactive wizards, and intuitive conventions that rely on human judgment. Agent-friendly tools instead emphasize non-interactive, scriptable interfaces with strict schemas, predictable CLI flags, and structured outputs like JSON alongside meaningful exit codes.

Feedback loops also change fundamentally. Rather than vague error messages meant for a human to search online, tools need concise, self-contained diagnostics that explain both what failed and how to fix it, allowing an agent to recover autonomously. Documentation shifts from sprawling prose to compact, up-to-date, machine-readable references and typed contracts that maximize signal within limited context windows. Finally, because agents iterate rapidly and occasionally make mistakes, good experience requires strong safety rails: idempotent operations, dry-run modes, cheap sandboxes, and fast, deterministic verification so agents can test assumptions without risking irreversible damage.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Treating AI coding agents as primary users makes discoverability and feedback central to developer experience. An agent needs to find the project’s rules, learn which commands to run, and tell whether a change worked from the files and tools it can access. That raises the value of versioned instructions in the repo, runnable examples, and documented, noninteractive commands with stable inputs and outputs.

Feedback matters just as much. A test failure that names the affected file and explains what went wrong gives an agent a concrete next step. Fast, focused checks let it verify each change before moving on. Explicit permissions and approval points define what it can do on its own, while diffs and execution logs give people a way to review what happened.

Many of these features already help human developers. Designing for agents makes them essential because agents depend on the environment to surface conventions, constraints, and evidence of success.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Treating AI coding agents as primary users changes the test for a good developer experience. Can an agent discover what a tool does, use it correctly, and verify the result without a human interpreting each step?

That makes interface details matter differently. A confirmation dialog gives a person control but can leave an unattended agent stuck. An explicit approval step lets the agent request a decision and resume afterward. Likewise, a stable CLI or API, documented defaults, structured output, and errors that explain how to recover make it easier for an agent to act reliably. A dry run lets it check the likely effect before changing anything.

The human experience still matters, especially when someone delegates work. A good tool makes permissions easy to set, consequential changes easy to review, and outcomes easy to verify.
